caption: Figure 1 Looping can improve data and compute efficiency (in over-trained regimes) while retaining downstream quality. We compare Vanilla (no looping), Standard Looping (repeatedly applying the same Transformer sequentially), and our modified versions Parallel Loop Transformer (PLT) (Wu et al., 2025) and Looped Transformers. Left: for 1B models trained across TPP 10–160, all looping methods achieve a given DCLM (Li et al., 2024) bits-per-byte (BPB) value with fewer training tokens than the fitted Vanilla baseline, with the modified PLT variants providing the largest relative data-efficiency gains. Center: across model sizes from 100M to 1B, we compare Vanilla models trained at TPP = 160 with two-loop models trained at TPP = 80. All looping methods achieve a given DCLM BPB with fewer training FLOPs than the fitted Vanilla baseline, and the modified PLT and Looped variants are more efficient than Standard Looping. Right: for 1B models across TPP 10–160, looping retains or improves mean NLL-ranked accuracy across eight reasoning and question-answering tasks; the modified PLT variants match or exceed Standard Looping. See Appendix D for the efficiency calculation and task-level results.

Figure 2 Looping designs: what is repeated, where, and in what order. Top: the looped component can be the complete transformer block, attention alone, the MLP alone, or attention and the MLP separately. Bottom: full-stack looping traverses the complete transformer for L loops, whereas per-layer looping completes L loops of each block before advancing to the next. Middle-stack and middle-layer looping restrict the corresponding schedule to the central blocks. For a model containing B blocks, the first and last ⌊B/3⌋blocks are run once.

Figure 3 Full-Stack Looping is favored under fixed parameter-count and training-data budgets, whereas Middle-Stack Looping is favored under FLOP constraints. DCLM validation BPB versus the number of loops or total training FLOPs for 100M and 500M models. Each panel holds the model size and training-data budget constant, so the differences reflect how each strategy uses the additional computation introduced by looping. The advantage of full-stack looping becomes clearer at larger model scales and training budgets. Middle-Stack Looping with fewer loops achieves lower BPB when compute is limited, whereas Full-Stack Looping can attain lower BPB when more compute is available. Increasing the number of loops does not improve quality indefinitely: the 100M results exhibit saturation, regression, and instability when more loops are used. Lower BPB is better; red triangles indicate unstable or clipped runs.

Figure 4 Three ways to vary weights across loops. All designs retain the same base weights. Loop LoRA gives each loop a separate low-rank adapter. Loop Matrix lets each loop learn a combination of these adapters, while Loop Softmax restricts this combination to be nonnegative and sum to one.

Figure 5 Loop-specific corrections become more useful with deeper looping while adding few parameters. DCLM BPB for 300M models with Full-Stack Looping at TPP 100. The left, middle, and right panels plot BPB against loop count, non-embedding parameter count, and total training FLOPs, respectively. The break in the logarithmic parameter axis shows both parameter ranges. FLOPs include the corrections and the training tokens allocated at TPP 100. Lower BPB is better.

Figure 6 PLT shifts the connection between loops across tokens. Loop ℓat token n receives the current-token embedding and the state from loop ℓ−1 at token n −1. KV sharing and G-SWA are omitted for clarity.

Figure 7 Separate normalization recovers much of the quality lost by the shifted transition. DCLM BPB for 200M models at TPP 40 and 80. Each raw panel is followed by its normalized counterpart. Except for Normalized Addition, normalized variants use separate RMS normalization and fixed 50/50 mixing. Red stars mark unstable runs clipped for visualization. Lower BPB is better.

Figure 8 Normalized shifted PLT retains the benefit of looping at 1B. DCLM BPB at TPP 10, 20, 40, and 80. Shifted and unshifted PLT use separate RMS normalization and a rank-8 linear gate. At L = 2, shifted PLT closely tracks the unshifted control and improves upon Full-Stack Looping; at L = 4, a clearer gap to the unshifted control remains. Lower BPB is better.

Figure 9 Raw scaling curves underlying the relative-efficiency analysis. We plot observed DCLM validation BPB together with unconstrained Vanilla scaling-law fits. Left: BPB as a function of actual training tokens for fixed 1B models across training-token budgets. Middle: BPB as a function of total training FLOPs across model families from 100M to 1B. Vanilla models use TPP = 160, whereas looping models use two loops and TPP = 80. Points show observed runs, connecting lines show empirical trajectories, and dashed black curves show fitted Vanilla scaling laws. Lower BPB is better.

Figure 10 Task-level NLL-ranked accuracy for the 1B models. Results are shown for ARC Easy, ARC Challenge, HellaSwag, PIQA, WinoGrande, OpenBookQA, CommonsenseQA, and Social IQA. For each question, the model predicts the candidate with the lowest token-normalized NLL. Dashed horizontal lines denote random-choice accuracy. Lines connect measured checkpoints and are not fitted scaling laws. Higher is better.

Figure 11 Candidate-normalized correct-answer NLL for the same eight tasks. Candidate scores are computed from token-normalized NLL and normalized across the available answers. This continuous metric measures how strongly the model prefers the correct answer relative to the alternatives, including changes that do not alter the top-ranked answer. Dashed lines show the random-choice value log C for a task with C candidates. Because choice counts and prompt formats differ, values should be compared within, rather than across, datasets. Lower is better.

Figure 12 MMLU and MMLU-Pro results for the 1B models. Top: macro-averaged NLL-ranked accuracy, where the predicted answer is the candidate with the lowest token-normalized NLL. Bottom: candidate-normalized correct-answer NLL. Accuracy remains near the respective random-choice baselines, while candidate-normalized correct-answer NLL remains at or above the random-choice reference, particularly on MMLU-Pro. Dashed lines denote random-choice performance. Higher accuracy and lower NLL are better.

The raw shifted model uses neither normalization nor a gate before combining its inputs. The normalized reference uses the rank-8 linear gate defined in subsection G.3. The y-axis uses logarithmic spacing, but the tick labels show the underlying RMS ratios, not their logarithms.

Table 1 Model configurations used in our experiments. Transformer layers give the number of Transformer blocks. Model width is the dimension of the representation passed between layers, and MLP width is the intermediate dimension of the SwiGLU MLP. Q/KV gives the numbers of query heads and key–value heads, respectively. The first parameter column excludes the input embedding and is used to assign the model label and set the training-token budget. The final column includes the input embedding and gives the total number of trainable parameters. Parameter counts are reported in millions. All models use a vocabulary of 128,256 tokens, a context length of 8,192, and an attention-head dimension of 128.
